name: CSRF Defense Patterns
tagline: Breaking the browser ambient-credential confused-deputy problem with SameSite cookies, Fetch Metadata (`Sec-Fetch-Site`), and HMAC-bound tokens.
purpose: Build a progressive mental model of CSRF defense—from why simple CORS requests bypass preflight and SameSite subdomain blind spots to defense-in-depth middleware.

spark.summary: CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery) tricks an authenticated user's browser into sending unintended state-changing requests to a target origin that automatically attaches ambient session cookies.

learningJourney.title: What is CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery)
learningJourney.explanation:
Web browsers automatically attach **ambient credentials** (session cookies, HTTP Basic Auth) to every request targeting an origin—regardless of which page initiated it. If a logged-in user visits `evil.com`, a hidden `<form action="https://bank.com/transfer" method="POST">` arrives at `bank.com` with the victim's valid session cookie.

**CSRF Defense** breaks this confused-deputy problem by requiring proof of **origin** or **intent** that a cross-site page cannot forge: `SameSite` cookie attributes, browser-enforced `Sec-Fetch-Site` Fetch Metadata headers, and unpredictable Synchronizer or HMAC-bound Double-Submit tokens.
learningJourney.purpose: The mechanism: understand how CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery) works from first principles.

learningJourney.title: Why Naive CORS & Raw Double-Submit Cookies Fail
learningJourney.explanation: Relying solely on CORS `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` fails because HTML `<form>` submissions and `fetch()` with `Content-Type: text/plain` are **simple requests** that skip CORS preflight completely. Similarly, `SameSite=Lax` treats sibling subdomains (`blog.example.com -> api.example.com`) as `same-site` (same eTLD+1) and still attaches cookies.

sectionDiagram.summary: Stacking __Host- SameSite=Lax cookies, Sec-Fetch-Site middleware, and Content-Type + HMAC token checks closes simple-request and subdomain bypasses.

ideas.title: Bypassing Naive CORS via text/plain Simple Request
ideas.description: A `POST /api/transfer` endpoint relied on CORS without checking `Content-Type`. An attacker sent `fetch(..., {credentials:'include', headers:{'Content-Type':'text/plain'}, body:'{...}'})`, skipping preflight and executing the transfer.

ideas.title: Subdomain Cookie Overwrite Defeated by HMAC Binding
ideas.description: An XSS on `blog.example.com` overwrote an unsigned CSRF cookie on `.example.com`. Binding the token via `HMAC(secret, sessionId + random)` with `__Host-` prefix closed the bypass.

learningJourney.title: How to implement Fetch Metadata & Constant-Time Token Checks
learningJourney.explanation:
1. **Keep `GET`/`HEAD` Read-Only**: Never mutate state on `GET` (`SameSite=Lax` sends cookies on top-level `GET` links).
2. **Enforce `Sec-Fetch-Site` + `Content-Type: application/json`**: Reject `cross-site` state changes (except explicit webhooks) and block `text/plain` / `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` on JSON APIs.
3. **Constant-Time Verification**: Validate Synchronizer or HMAC-bound tokens with `hmac.compare_digest` / `crypto.timingSafeEqual`, and mask tokens per-response (BREACH mitigation) when rendered inside compressed HTML.
learningJourney.markdownContent:
```python
# Fetch Metadata + Constant-Time HMAC CSRF Guard (Python)
import hmac, hashlib

def verify_csrf_request(headers: dict, session_id: str, secret: bytes) -> bool:
    # 1. Browser-enforced Fetch Metadata (cannot be spoofed by JS)
    fetch_site = headers.get('sec-fetch-site')
    if fetch_site == 'cross-site':
        return False
    # 2. Require explicit JSON Content-Type on API mutations
    if not headers.get('content-type', '').startswith('application/json'):
        return False
    # 3. Verify HMAC-bound X-CSRF-Token in constant time
    provided = headers.get('x-csrf-token', '')
    expected = hmac.new(secret, session_id.encode(), hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()
    return hmac.compare_digest(expected, provided)
```

learningJourney.title: Alternatives: SameSite vs. Fetch Metadata vs. Synchronizer vs. Double-Submit
learningJourney.explanation: Each defense layer has distinct state requirements, subdomain coverage, and legacy browser trade-offs.

benefits: `Lax` preserves inbound links from email/Slack while blocking cross-site `POST` forms.
costs: `Strict` breaks inbound links (users appear logged out); neither blocks sibling subdomains (`eTLD+1`).

benefits: Zero server state; cleanly distinguishes `same-origin` vs `same-site` vs `cross-site`.
costs: Old browsers/proxies may strip `Sec-Fetch-*`—pair with `Origin` or token fallback.

benefits: Zero extra cookies; trivially invalidated on logout; BREACH-masked.
Stateless (works with JWT-in-cookie) while preventing subdomain cookie-planting.
costs: Must bind token to `HttpOnly` session ID via server HMAC key.
